newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call money ends down, gilts mixed.
newsitem.headline: Indian call money ends down, gilts mixed.

text.p: Indian call money ended Wednesday at 4.25 percent, down from the day's opening 5.0-5.25 percent on reduced demand for funds, dealers said.
They said there were few borrowers left in the market by late morning and rates eased as the supply of funds was good.
"Banks are sitting on a comfortable pile of funds," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "With supply good and demand not very high, call money will remain easy."
Dealers said prices of government securities ended mixed in moderate trade.
"Prices of some securities fell but by and large the market was steady today," said a dealer. "There was some demand for treasury bills which pushed prices up."

The 13.50 percent 1998 government of India stock traded on Wednesday at 102.85 rupees against its latest traded price of 103.08 while the zero percent 1999 stock was unchanged at 77.75 rupees, they said.

The treasury bill maturing on January 2, 1998 was traded at a yield of 10.30 on Wednesday against its last traded yield of 10.35 percent while the bill maturing on December 19 yielded 10.30 percent against 10.25, dealers said.
Dealers said the announcement of a new loan issue for January 20 was a signal that long-term interest rates were coming down.
The finance ministry announced on Wednesday that 25 state governments would issue 16.09 billion rupees worth of 13.75 percent 10-year stock on January 20.
"This represents a 25 basis point drop from the 14 percent 10-year stock issued last year," said Aashsih Pitale, manager debt research at ICICI Securities and Finance Company.
"Even in the current financial year, the last issue of 10-year stock was at 13.85 percent," he said.
Dealers said there were no trades in commercial paper or certificates of deposit on Wednesday.
